senses.gloss: Old and deserving respect.

contrast: Modern American usage says *sexually transmitted* instead — an STD, an STI. *Venereal* now sounds old-fashioned or clinical.

examples: *Venereal* disease was a taboo subject for decades.
The clinic treats *venereal* infections free of charge.
The old textbook has a chapter on *venereal* warts.

senses.ru: с полностью наступившими правами (о пенсионном плане)

form: from *vestige* — a small trace of something that is gone

senses.gloss: Left over from an earlier stage and no longer of any use.
examples: The appendix is a *vestigial* organ.

contrast: *A veteran* standing alone is a noun — someone who served in the military.

senses.gloss: Having done a job for many years.
examples: She's a *veteran* reporter at the paper.
The team signed a *veteran* pitcher for one more season.
*Veteran* teachers usually get the harder classes.

contrast: The person is a *veterinarian*, or a *vet* for short — *veterinary* is only the adjective.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the medical care of animals.
examples: He's studying *veterinary* medicine at Cornell.

senses.gloss: Argued over for years without an answer, said of a question.

contrast: A *vexing* problem annoys you; a *vexed* person is the one who is annoyed.

senses.gloss: Annoying and hard to settle.

senses.gloss: Able to work and succeed.

senses.gloss: Able to live and keep growing.

senses.gloss: Full of life and energy.

senses.gloss: Bright and strong, said of a color.

senses.gloss: Felt by watching someone else do it rather than doing it yourself.

senses.gloss: Having to do with a vice president or that office.

senses.gloss: Cruel and violent.

senses.gloss: Meant to hurt someone with words.

senses.gloss: Very severe or painful.

senses.gloss: Having won a fight, a game or an election.

position: both — always with a capital V

senses.gloss: Strong and full of physical energy.

senses.gloss: Extremely unpleasant.

senses.gloss: Very strong and sudden.

contrast: *A violet* is also the small flower, and the color is the bluer end of purple.

senses.gloss: Existing on a computer or a network rather than in the real world.

senses.gloss: Almost what you would call it, though not officially so.

examples: I'm *wary* of deals that sound too good.
The dog is *wary* around strangers.
She grew *warier* with every question he asked.

senses.gloss: Able to be washed without being damaged.
examples: The whole cover is *washable*.
Buy a *washable* rug if you have a dog.
*Washable* paint comes off the wall with water.

form: compound — from the phrasal verb *wash out*

senses.gloss: Faded, with the color gone.
examples: He wore *washed-out* jeans and a gray T-shirt.
The photo is *washed-out* and yellow at the edges.

senses.gloss: Pale and tired.
examples: She looked *washed-out* after the night shift.
Everyone feels a little *washed-out* in February.

contrast: Informal and unkind, and always about a career — it has nothing to do with washing.

senses.gloss: Finished, with no chance of succeeding again.
examples: At thirty-four the sportswriters called him *washed-up*.
He plays a *washed-up* actor trying for a comeback.
She was *washed-up* in Hollywood before she turned thirty.

contrast: The third sense is slang and rude — keep it for friends.

senses.gloss: Used badly, or used for nothing.
examples: It was a *wasted* trip — the office was closed.
Those were three *wasted* years of my life.

senses.gloss: Thin and weak from illness or hunger.
examples: His arms were *wasted* after months in bed.
The photographs show *wasted* faces staring at the camera.

senses.gloss: Very drunk or high.
examples: Half the party was *wasted* by midnight.
He got *wasted* at his own wedding.

senses.gloss: Using more of something than is needed.
examples: Running the dishwasher half full is *wasteful*.
The old furnace is *wasteful* of fuel.
They cut the most *wasteful* programs first.

contrast: *Under the watchful eye of* is the phrase you will meet most often.

senses.gloss: Paying close attention to what is happening.
examples: The kids swam under the *watchful* eye of a lifeguard.
She stayed *watchful* the whole drive home.
He's more *watchful* than he used to be.

contrast: *Water-repellent* sheds light rain, *water-resistant* holds water out for a while, *waterproof* keeps it all out.

senses.gloss: Treated so that water runs off instead of soaking in.
examples: The jacket has a *water-repellent* finish.
Spray the boots to make them *water-repellent*.
*Water-repellent* fabric is not the same as waterproof.

contrast: *Water-resistant* is weaker than *waterproof* — don't swim in a *water-resistant* watch.

senses.gloss: Able to keep water out for a while, though not completely.
examples: The watch is *water-resistant* to fifty meters.
Get a *water-resistant* case for your phone.
This coat is more *water-resistant* than my old one.

senses.gloss: Able to dissolve in water.
examples: Vitamin C is *water-soluble*, so the body doesn't store it.
Use a *water-soluble* glue for the paper models.
The pills come in a *water-soluble* coating.

form: compound — *water* + *borne*, carried; one word in American English

senses.gloss: Carried by water, said of a disease.
examples: Cholera is a *waterborne* disease.
The flood raised the risk of *waterborne* illness.

senses.gloss: Carried on water, said of goods or travel.
examples: *Waterborne* freight is far cheaper than trucking.
The city grew on *waterborne* trade.

senses.gloss: So full of water that it cannot hold any more.
examples: The field was *waterlogged* and the game was called off.
*Waterlogged* soil kills most roots in a week.
The boat sat low in the water, *waterlogged* and useless.
